summary:
Victoria's anti-vilification regime is set by the Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025 and assented to on 8 April 2025. It inserts civil vilification protections into the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and criminal protections into the Crimes Act 1958, repealing the existing racial and religious tolerance statute, and is directed at equal participation and public safety. Vilification on the grounds of gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation carries up to five years' imprisonment, with political, religious and academic exemptions; the criminal provisions take effect on 30 June 2026.

Gender identity has been a prohibited ground of discrimination in Victoria since 2000, under the Equal Opportunity (Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation) Act 2000 amending the Equal Opportunity Act 1995, and was retained in the replacement Equal Opportunity Act 2010. Sex characteristics were added as a protected attribute effective 2021, and the Justice Legislation Amendment (Police and Other Matters) Act passed in September 2022 extended protection to on-duty Victoria Police officers on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds.

Religious exemptions have been narrowed but not eliminated. The Equal Opportunity (Religious Exceptions) Amendment Act 2021, effective 15 June 2022, bars religious schools and organisations from discriminating against employees because of sexual orientation, gender identity or marital status, and bars government-funded bodies from refusing services on those grounds, except where conformity with doctrine is an inherent requirement of the job, such as hiring a religious studies teacher. Exemptions remain under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 for religious organisations including adoption and fostering agencies and charities that receive no government funding, allowing them to discriminate against LGBT employees and clients.

Victoria prohibits conversion practices. The Change or Suppression (Conversion) Practices Prohibition Act passed the lower house 55-0 in December 2020 and the Legislative Council 27-9 on 5 February 2021, with penalties of up to approximately $200,000 AUD or ten years' imprisonment, taking effect in February 2022, one year after royal assent. It followed the Health Complaints Act, effective 1 February 2017, which empowered the Health Complaints Commissioner to issue warnings and temporary or permanent practice bans after a May 2018 investigation.

Gender transition is legally recognised by Victoria. Birth certificates are issued by the state Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, and since November 2025 updated regulations removed all fees and costs for an application to change sex on a birth certificate. Victorian driver licences carry no recorded gender marker. Earlier law required a person to be unmarried and to undergo sexual reassignment surgery before changing recorded sex; the unmarried requirement, which had been due to lapse in December 2018, was removed early by Parliament in May 2018, while an August 2016 bill to remove the surgery requirement and allow parents to alter a child's gender descriptor with the child's informed consent failed. Passports and marriage remain Commonwealth matters.

Victoria is the only Australian state to maintain an LGBTIQA+ Commissioner. The office dates from the appointment of an inaugural Gender and Sexuality Commissioner in July 2015, charged with aligning Commonwealth and state records on passports and birth certificates and strengthening workplace protections for transgender workers; it was later renamed Commissioner for LGBTIQ+ Communities. Joe Ball, a transgender man, was appointed on 23 September 2024 for a three-year term to advise government on safe and inclusive policies, services and programs and to lead implementation of Pride in our Future, Victoria's ten-year LGBTIQA+ equality plan.

A Victorian coroner investigating the suicides of five young transgender women recommended urgent investment in health care for trans and gender-diverse people; ABC News reported the findings on 29 August 2024. The state government says it is reviewing the recommendations, and local advocacy groups will press for their implementation.

On care for trans young people, the Supreme Court of Victoria upheld in August 2024 the availability of puberty blockers for transgender children experiencing stress and anxiety.
tangentialFactors:
Within Australia, vilification coverage by gender identity differs sharply between states: Victoria's 2025 Act adds gender identity, sex and sex characteristics alongside sexual orientation, while several states confine vilification law to sexual orientation and others cover none of these grounds. The Victorian criminal offences do not commence until 30 June 2026, so the timing of any complaint matters.

Funding cuts have been reported as risking a backlog at the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission, established in 1975, which is the body受理 complaints of discrimination and vilification. Delay there affects how quickly any Victorian remedy is delivered.
localsOnly:
Victoria's Relationships Act, passed on 10 April 2008, has allowed domestic relationships to be registered since 1 December 2008, a state-level record separate from Commonwealth marriage status.

Victoria was the first Australian state to create an expungement scheme for historical offences relating to consensual same-sex conduct that are no longer criminal. Passed on 15 October 2014 and effective from 1 September 2015, it allows an individual, or a representative of a deceased person, to apply to the Secretary of the Department of Justice and Regulation; a successful application means the person may lawfully claim not to have been convicted and the conviction does not appear on a police records check, avoiding travel and employment consequences. A formal parliamentary apology followed on 24 May 2016.

Residents, as well as visitors, can lodge complaints under the Equal Opportunity Act 2010 and, once commenced on 30 June 2026, under the new civil vilification provisions, through the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Victorian source in the inventory addresses the placement of transgender prisoners in state corrective facilities, so that question is unresolved here rather than answered.

Whether the criminal vilification offences commenced as scheduled on 30 June 2026 is not confirmed by any source held; the inventory supplies the commencement date only.

Whether the state government has adopted the coroner's recommendations on trans health-care investment is unresolved: the government states a review is under way and advocacy groups are pressing for implementation, with no outcome sourced.

The reported funding cuts to the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission and their effect on complaint handling are sourced only as a reported risk of backlog, not as a measured delay.

No source in the inventory documents airport or border treatment of trans travellers through Victorian terminals, or access to gendered facilities in Victorian venues, so those points remain unsourced for this state.
